title: ‘Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass’ Review: The Famous Cat-and-Mouse Duo Are Not Themselves In a Chaotic Chinese Cartoon
description: That title gives a first clue towards how misbegotten and compromised this new Tom and Jerry joint is. Everybody knows that Tom and Jerry shouldn’t
body: That title gives a first clue towards how misbegotten and compromised this new Tom and Jerry joint is. Everybody knows that Tom and Jerry shouldn’t be searching for a forbidden compass, whatever that might be: If the perma-warring pair are on a quest for something, it ought to be, say, some pickles for a big cheese sandwich. The Hanna-Barbera cat and mouse — formerly a throwaway bunch of cartoons, now a ‘franchise’ — are all about triflingly menial disputes taken to absurd heights, leading to surreal sight gags and baroque violence.“Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass” gives us the most cursory of tributes to that mode in the film’s opening five minutes, as Jerry heads to a grand exhibition in New York called “Traveling Exhibition of the Astral Compass – Journey to the Enigmatic East.” (Edward Said fans are advised to bring bingo cards.) Tom is a security guard here, and forbids entrance to the little mouse, leading to a brief spate of chasing around the museum. This hubbub somehow awakens the mysterious powers of the titular compass, transporting the twosome to ‘Golden City’ in China, modeled after the Forbidden City, where a storyline based on Chinese mythology is about to get going. That is where all classic Tom and Jerry tomfoolery ends — and there are another 95 minutes to go.In Golden City we meet a character called Phoenix Master and his irritating sidekick Feeny, who resembles a thicc Big Bird with green hair coiffed à la Liberace. They have been sent down from heaven by the Celestial Master and must therefore find the compass again, with the aid of some anthropomorphic traditional roof decorations, such as ‘Sonny’, a green and pink icon of a god, or ‘Xander’, a horse-like creature. But in order to get the compass, they will have to defeat ‘Mega-Rat’, the movie’s villain, who labours away in a cave with his evil henchrats.That précis will give some idea of the alarming mental disconnect that the film puts viewers through, as it tosses Tom and indeed Jerry into this incomprehensible plot, in which the title characters will soon be reduced to the status of glorified onlookers. But before that, there’s time for a smattering of creaky scenes in which the Chinese characters mistake the American interlopers for deities and give them a sponsored-by-the-Tourism-Board visit of the premises. (“Ah, Golden Lake — when the spring flowers bloom, people come from all over! Isn’t it a beautiful sight?”) Some viewers may at this point be put in mind of “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom” — another tick on your Orientalism card, if you’re playing.The Chinese characters are animated in standard-issue knock-off Pixar mode, and therefore match up just about with Tom and Jerry 2.0, but the visuals around them are ceaselessly incoherent, adding to the already harrowing levels of chaos. Chinese traditional landscape painting commingles with manga-like warfare and knockabout gags Hollywood-style, and in the background of all the migraine-inducingly hyperactive shenanigans, there appear some upsettingly undifferentiated crowds of AI-faced villagers saying ‘rhubarb rhubarb’ to one another.Throughout, Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass feels bafflingly out of touch and off-key, with the flavor of supermarket own-brand cornflakes. To wit, a montage in which Tom and Jerry eat a buffet of noodles and dumplings while someone or other raps, “Tom and Jerry, you and I/We’re gonna make a million, gonna touch the sky” may have the paradoxical effect of making children clamor for some soothingly 2D cartoons from the 1940s.The film’s casual use of deeply American IP in order to sell what is unmistakably a Chinese property — produced by the state-owned China Film Group in partnership with Warner Bros. and Origin Animation — may be of interest to future students of geopolitics, but even as a spectacle for kids weaned on flashing lights and brainrot it is likely to be too jumbled and bewildering. As for the parent demographic, it will only appeal to that rare subset who actively dislike their children.

schema.headline: ‘Tom and Jerry: Forbidden Compass’ Review: The Famous Cat-and-Mouse Duo Are Not Themselves In a Chaotic Chinese Cartoon

title: Robert Pattinson Wants Chris Hansen to Like ‘Primetime’ Despite His Criticisms: ‘I Hope the Inspiration His Character Has Given Is Some Kind of Compliment’
description: Robert Pattinson hopes Chris Hansen is a fan “Primetime,” a tense thriller about the television journalist and “To Catch a Predator” host, which pre
body:
Robert Pattinson hopes Chris Hansen is a fan “Primetime,” a tense thriller about the television journalist and “To Catch a Predator” host, which premieres on Saturday afternoon at the Venice Film Festival. 

	The real-life Hansen has been vocal about his take on the movie, which he said he hasn’t seen because he declined to sign A24‘s standard NDA. But Hansen said that based on the trailer, he finds Pattinson’s portrayal “overly dramatic.” (However, he admitted that his family “seem to think it’s a pretty good imitation.”)
	

	“Obviously, I hope he likes the movie,” Pattinson said on Saturday’s Venice Film Festival press conference. “There’s something electrifying about him. I would hope the amount of inspiration his character has given a lot of people for years is some kind of compliment.”


	Directed by Lance Oppenheim in his narrative feature debut, “Primetime” is set in the mid-2000s and follows Hansen, then the host of Dateline NBC’s “To Catch a Predator,” as he turns the pursuit of suspected child predators into primetime entertainment. Loosely based on the 2007 “Esquire” article “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die,” the movie exposes the ethical limits of Hansen’s methods and the collision between journalism, policing and entertainment. “To Catch a Predator” ultimately ended in 2008 after facing some backlash over its methods of confronting the suspects.

	“There’s something magnetic about his presence. I watched the show when I was younger and didn’t think about it,” Pattinson said. “There’s a strange alchemy — something he’s doing is the reason people are still talking about that show 20 years later. It’s not to do solely with the subject matter. It was something about the show that was groundbreaking, but then he’s someone centering it. There’s something, even after watching literally thousands of hours of it, you can’t put your finger on it.”
	

	Before “Primetime” premieres in competition at the Venice Film Festival, Pattinson was joined at Saturday’s press conference by Oppenheim and co-stars Skyler Gisondo, Merritt Wever and Phoebe Bridgers. Pattinson praised Bridgers, the Grammy-winning singer and songwriter who makes her acting debut in “Primetime.”

	“She’s unbelievable,” Pattinson said. “I didn’t even know Lance and Phoebe were friends. When he suggested her, I was like ‘Phoebe Bridgers? Why don’t we get the Queen?’ Even on the first day, she was so relaxed. She didn’t seem nervous at all. She completely got the tone, and it’s a relatively difficult movie.”

	Bridgers, for her part, described the filming process as “super intimidating.”

	“When Lance asked me, I was like, ‘No way, dude,'” she remembers. “But it turns out, working with incredible people actually makes it way easier. I thought I was going to wither with all of these guys. Instead, it was just fun and free.”

	Oppenheim previously directed the documentaries “Some Kind of Heaven,” “Spermworld” and the HBO series “Ren Faire.” Following its debut in competition on the Lido, “Primetime” will be released theatrically by A24 on Sept. 25. Oppenheim, who is 30, remembers discovering “To Catch a Predator,” not through the show itself but through parodies on “South Park” and comedy website Ebaum’s World.

	“When I finally saw ‘To Catch a Predator,’ I was amazed,” Oppenheim said. “Chris Hansen had these one-liners like Tony Montana. I was always fascinated by the theatricality of the show. ‘What happens when you turn one of the darkest subjects known to humankind into entertainment?'”

	More to come…

title: Marion Cotillard Praises Venice Biennale College Cinema Workshop: ‘Not all Films Are Destined to Draw Millions of Viewers and Turn a Profit’
description: Oscar-winner Marion Cotillard (“La Vie en Rose”) is at the Venice Film Festival in a new guise, as tutor of Biennale College Cinema, the workshop al
body:
Oscar-winner Marion Cotillard (“La Vie en Rose”) is at the Venice Film Festival in a new guise, as tutor of Biennale College Cinema, the workshop allowing emerging filmmakers to develop and produce micro-budget feature-length films, which is sponsored by Chanel.

	Biennale College Cinemas was conceived 15 years ago by Venice chief Alberto Barbera in tandem with Torino Film Lab topper Savina Neirotti, who heads the unique Venice initiative. 
	

	During this time Biennale College has spawned 49 feature film projects made with micro-budgets with grants that after the first decade rose from €150,00 ($174,00) to €200,00 ($232) during the past five years. “These works provide a bird’s eye view of what it means to debut as a filmmaker today,” Neirotti noted.


	“When Chanel told me about this program, I was very touched,” said Cotillard. “Above all, I think it’s very important to support films that are struggling to get off the ground financially these days,” she added.

	“Not all films are destined to draw millions of viewers and turn a profit, and I think it’s very important to support artists — artists from all over the world – some of whom, even in their own countries, simply don’t have access to production opportunities,” she noted. 

	“And what’s really striking about the films I’ve seen — the four films I’ve seen – is their artistic passion; that need to tell stories,” Cotillard continued. 

	This year’s Biennale College projects, all first works, hail from China, Italy, Mexico, Spain and the U.S. They are: “Demeter in Exile,” by Italian director Maria Giovanna Cicciari who is teamed wth producer Raffaella Pontarelli. “Gu Shi” by Chinese director Yinan Song and produced by Yueyi Xing; “Moonfish,” by U.S. director Daniel Zvereff who is teamed with Spanish producer Mireia Villanova; and “Tijuana Todavía” by Mexian director Gabriel Gutierrez Morales working with producer Humberto Busto Marín.
	

	Barbera also said he will soon be announcing the winner of the first edition of Biennale College Blend, the initiative’s new strand for artists looking to explore stories in the multi-media space comprising forms of expression such as music, visual arts, and performing arts.

schema.headline: Marion Cotillard Praises Venice Biennale College Cinema Workshop: ‘Not all Films Are Destined to Draw Millions of Viewers and Turn a Profit’

title: ‘Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?’ Review: An Assaultive Yet Turgid and Outdated Vietnam PTSD Drama
description: If Shinya Tsukamoto‘s “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” were the first, or even the 51st, movie to litigate the atrocities committed by U.S. troops
body:
If Shinya Tsukamoto‘s “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” were the first, or even the 51st, movie to litigate the atrocities committed by U.S. troops during the Vietnam War, perhaps on a purely informational level some justification would exist for its crudely simplistic approach. Nuance is often a casualty of war, especially when that war is ongoing or recently ended. But this is 2026, when — in contrast to the era in which the real, evidently heroic Allen Nelson, on whose memoir the film is based, toured his cautionary horror story internationally — you’d be hard pressed to find a substantial contingent unaware that the Vietnam War has since been judged a mistake so costly in human life and dignity that it forced arguably the most substantial reevaluation of American self-identity since independence.
	

	Even still, reliving the dehumanizing cruelty of conflict and working through its aftermath might be a valuable exercise if new insights, uncovered through this one man’s PTSD journey, could then be scaled up and applied to the national psyche. And revisiting Vietnam through the eyes of a Black American, via the outsider perspective of the Japanese director of “Tetsuo: The Iron Man,” no less, must surely deliver some new insights? But despite half taking place in a therapist’s office, “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” is only invested in its lead’s psychology insofar as it provides the excuse for a series of increasingly grisly and violent flashbacks, and has nothing but the most cursory and stereotype-laden interest in the effect of the war on the African-American community specifically.
	

	Marine Allen Nelson (played by Mark Merphy as a younger man and Rodney Hicks as his older counterpart) has recently returned from the front in severe shellshock. Unwilling to subject his family to his bouts of paranoia and rage, he is dossing in a filthy, boarded-up building in New York City, with only a straggly cat and the fat, oily alley rats for company. Furtively darting out to shoplift some supplies one day, he is accosted by an old classmate who brightly announces she is now a schoolteacher and invites him to speak about his war experiences to her class. He demurs initially. 

	But then, some boys throw bangers nearby, and he finds himself diving for cover under a nearby car, where, in one of the film’s more effectively abstract evocations of a dissociative episode, he watches the slice of pavement visible from his vantage point reverberating to the deafening chaos of explosions and gunfire in his mind. He shows up at the class, lathered in sweat (the sweat-spray and gunshot-squib cost for this film must represent a sizeable portion of its budget) and hesitantly begins to speak. But he is unable to answer the moppet who — in a sentimental, heavily-leaned-into close-up — poses the question that gave Nelson’s original memoir, and gives Tsukamoto’s film, its name.

	Years later, Nelson is married to Linda (pity poor Tatyana Ali, saddled with an almost comically underwritten, saintly-supportive-partner role) and is raising her son as his own. But he cannot sleep without medication to suppress his violent nightmares. After a particularly troubling outburst, he goes into therapy and, piece by piece, tells his story to Dr Daniels (Geoffrey Rush). These flashbacks betray where writer-director-cinematographer-editor Tsukamoto’s filmmaking interests really lie, which is in the gruesome recreation of hideous acts of barbarism and cruelty. Some of those, for good measure, he cuts into a montage, alongside rats gnawing on maggoty flesh and piles of moldering corpses, to deploy whenever things get boring back in one of the brown rooms of Allen’s present life. So, quite often.

	It is deeply unsavory that a film with such a ploddingly earnest anti-war message only comes alive in the depiction of violent, brutal death. As if aware of that, Tsukamoto seem to arrange the non-combat scenes as a penance, as though we, like the protagonist, must atone for the base thrills of warfare with endless tedious talk sessions. Hicks is a Broadway actor of some standing, but it’s very hard to tell here given that the ESL-style screenplay leaves him no register to work in other than sweatily anguished or, occasionally, sweatily relieved and illuminated in one of the rare shafts of sunlight allowed to penetrate Tsukamoto’s penumbral images.
	

	Rush, bringing what gravitas he can to a role that is essentially a dark brown sweater with eyes, compensates for essentially only having one line of dialogue (“Why did you kill people, Allen?”) by repeating it approximately one million times with slight variations of emphasis and formulation, until it finally elicits the breakthrough Allen needs. Beware this false dawn, however. It may have taken an eternity to get to, but this is only the first of many natural cutoff points where Tsukamoto could have put us out of our and Allen’s misery, only to instead fade up into yet another epilogue. 

	The film has maybe eight or ten endings — forgive the inexactness, you too may lose track of the number of times you are halfway out of your seat with one arm in the sleeve of your coat, before realizing that no, that very obvious dramatic beat was not the final bow, because now, suddenly Allen has a beard and a daughter! Oh, now his beard is gray. Oh, now he’s on a boat! And here is Lily Franky, the great Japanese actor who is fourth-billed but arrives at the eleventh hour to deliver a single monologue to a closed bathroom door. It is rare to come across a film — especially in a major festival’s competition lineup — in which not only does so little work, it is given such endless acreage in which to keep not working, which is especially striking given that there’s little in “Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?” that can’t be boiled down to: “Yes, I did.”

schema.headline: ‘Mr Nelson, Did You Kill People?’ Review: An Assaultive Yet Turgid and Outdated Vietnam PTSD Drama

title: ‘The Liberation’ Review: Carrie Coon Is Breathtaking as a Woman Lured by a Cult in Guy Nattiv’s Deeply Personal Film
description: “You carry a lot of weight around, don’t you?” In Guy Nattiv’s observant, harrowing and unmistakably feminine “The Liberation,” this line marks the
body:
“You carry a lot of weight around, don’t you?” In Guy Nattiv’s observant, harrowing and unmistakably feminine “The Liberation,” this line marks the first time someone truly sees through fortysomething protagonist Rita Cooper. Based on Nattiv’s own grandmother (alongside various cult survivors) and played by Carrie Coon with extraordinary emotional presence and pent-up energy privately looking for an outlet, Rita is an early-1980s woman leading an ordinary life in New Jersey. Quietly depressed, a wife to Reuben (Tracy Letts, Coon’s real-life partner) and mother to Ella (Bella Ramsey) and Jo (Odessa Young), Rita holds a monotonous desk job at a bank by day, and tends to her family by night as part of her humdrum routine. Elsewhere, she agrees to be a part of a video project as a Holocaust survivor, an identity that has defined her past and continues to seep into her present in private, guilt-ridden ways.
	

	She is confronted with that question at her workplace by the mysterious Ricki (Lily James), an intriguing young woman with an uneasy edge looking to deposit a surprisingly hefty sum of money. Rita shrugs it off with a throwaway remark about her middle-aged metabolism, while handling Ricki’s business. But Ricki isn’t talking about the weight women routinely pressure ourselves about. She’s played with a darkly enigmatic, unnerving quality by James in her finest work to date — a knowing, even domineering smile often curling around her lips. Her next question: “When was the last time you saw the sunset on a beach?”


	Ricki is a cult leader in plainest terms, setting her predatory sights on Rita as her next recruit. As these cult stories tend to go, there is usually a magnetic male leader at the center, a sexual predator who brainwashes and preys on young women in search of direction. The scenario in “The Liberation” isn’t that at all — it actually feels several shades darker and more frightening than those clichés, as any middle-aged woman like this critic will feel in their bones. 
	

	Rita is at a point in her life when she’s settled into what she deems a less-than-ideal reality, realizing there won’t be anything more. She also feels like her body, her age and her reflection in the mirror are all collectively betraying her, another recognizable truth in her life. So what can possibly feel better and safer than the warm blanket that is female camaraderie, the allyship of fellow women who know exactly what Ricki is going through? Perhaps this is finally a chance for her to free herself from her past, from all society’s preconceived notions and expectations. If only Ricki’s intentions were pure.

	Co-written by Noa Berman Herzberg, this is a deeply personal story for writer-director Nattiv, and he does unwavering justice to the shared universality of Rita’s womanly journey. Operating on two timelines that are edited with conviction and well-paced clarity by Sabine Hoffman and Yuval Orr, “The Liberation” introduces us to a Rita deeply caught in Ricki’s web at first, with her daughters Ella and Jo risking a long, perilous journey to rescue their mother from a commune somewhere in the woods. 

	One of the best actors working today, Coon essentially plays two different sides of Rita with astonishing range across these chronologies, portraying the past and the present of her character through distinctive markers. The domestic Rita is frazzled, hesitant, unsure of her place in the world. Dressed in muted florals and wearing a tranquil attitude on her sleeve, the commune Rita (now named Naia) is contrastingly at peace, yet alarmingly docile, eating a deficient diet of plants (sometimes of the hallucinatory kind), no longer smoking or pill-popping.

	Nattiv skilfully braids together the key events that lead to Rita’s breakdown, with a breathtaking sense of tension across the flashbacks. At each turn, a heartbreaking picture comes into sharper focus, underscoring Ricki’s destructive appetite that exploits Rita’s deepest needs and fears under the guise of friendship and no-judgement sisterhood. It’s scary stuff to hear Rita recite lines straight out of today’s empty therapy-speak, delivered by Coon with a devastating sense of vulnerability. 

	DPs Fabian Gamper and Tudor Vladimir Panduru’s grainy lensing poetically captures these intimate faultlines and era-specific textures, staying close to Rita’s face and increasingly hazy eyes. In their hands, “The Liberation” almost looks like secretly filmed archival footage, with an early-’80s aesthetic still carrying traces of the ‘70s. Their work is matched by the production design and costuming details that favor a real, lived-in version of the decade without caricatured colors and eye-popping patterns.
	

	The film’s absorbing final act is when Nattiv switches gears towards a more conventionally nail-biting thriller, with a diabetic Jo being put in harm’s way by the commune — it would be up to her sister and mother to save her. It’s an elegantly gripping turn in a patient and graceful film that generously laments the pain of an unfulfilled woman.

schema.headline: ‘The Liberation’ Review: Carrie Coon Is Breathtaking as a Woman Lured by a Cult in Guy Nattiv’s Deeply Personal Film

title: Rubaiyat Hossain on Bodies, Beauty and Venice, Toronto and London-Bound ‘The Difficult Bride,’ Clip Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The idea for “The Difficult Bride” traces back to a story Rubaiyat Hossain heard as a 7 year old, visiting a Dhaka beauty parlor with her mother.
body:
The idea for “The Difficult Bride” traces back to a story Rubaiyat Hossain heard as a 7 year old, visiting a Dhaka beauty parlor with her mother.

	“There was a bride who died there,” Hossain says. “Everyone knew this story from our generation, and I remember being seven, and even at that time, I had visualized this story. It was in sepia for some reason, I don’t know, but I completely had the visuals in my head, and it’s something that always stayed with me.”
	

	Variety is unveiling an exclusive clip from the supernatural feminist drama, which will become the first Bangladeshi feature to screen at the Venice Film Festival when it bows in the Horizons competition.


	That salon, Mayfair, became the setting for a film that follows Zaineen (Zaineen Chowdhury Karim), a bride-to-be whose wedding preparations spiral into a battle with her own body. Hossain first tried the material as a short in 2006. Two decades and many drafts later, the project pulled in her academic background in gender studies alongside something more personal. “My own self and my own body became a part of the film,” she says. “My embodied experience of being a female in my own body and how I feel is something I tried to communicate in the film. And that is why it became supernatural, because a lot of the things are not logical. That is where the grotesque comes in, that is where the lizards and the snakes come in.”

	Hossain is careful not to place the blame for that pressure solely on men. Azmeri Haque Badhon plays the salon owner who enforces the beauty standard on Zaineen, including a scene of facial injections that Hossain says mirrors treatment common in Bangladeshi salons. “It’s also about how women can be some of the biggest upholders and sustainers of patriarchy and the patriarchal system,” she says. “It’s not only men; women also participate in this. It’s a system of power. It takes both to participate in it.”
	

	The film’s Dhaka backdrop carries traces of the country’s July 2024 unrest, including scenes of women being surveilled and policed for their clothing and behavior, work that reaches the screen through Rikita Nondine Shimu’s character, Minoti. Hossain resists reading the film as a direct response to that period, though. “I wouldn’t say the film is set around the time of July,” she says. “I tried to create like a reality of Dhaka where there is political violence outside, there is a lot of violence against women. Women’s rights have always been an issue in Bangladesh.”

	She places “The Difficult Bride” alongside her earlier features as a kind of class trilogy of Bangladeshi womanhood. “‘Under Construction’ talked about a middle-class woman, ‘Made in Bangladesh’ talked about a working-class woman, and I think ‘The Difficult Bride’ talks about the kind of the ultra-wealthy population of the tri-state,” she says, referring to Dhaka’s Gulshan-Baridhara area. “Even in this gilded cage, even with all these privileges, you can’t be free.”

	Karim, making her acting debut in the lead role, was originally Hossain’s assistant director. When the shoot’s original cast changed following the disruption from July, Karim stepped in to read opposite another actor during Zoom rehearsals. “She is so beautiful and I feel like she is the character herself,” Hossain says of watching her on screen. “I might have auditioned her like around 15, 20 times.” The cast also includes Sunerah Kamal in addition to Badhon and Shimu, all three of whom are Bangladesh National Film Award winners.

	Hossain, who teaches part-time at Smith College, including a course on love and devotion in Bollywood cinema, argues that the pressures her film dramatizes extend well beyond South Asia. “I see that a woman who is coming from Mexico or Guatemala or Bangladesh or Vermont have same issues when it comes to this specific idea of beauty and submitting,” she says.

	Offscreen, Hossain has launched a grant and mentorship program for Bangladeshi women filmmakers, aiming to address what she describes as compounding structural barriers: limited access to money, restrictions on women’s mobility, the absence of a formal film school and an industry culture built on informal, male peer networks. “There is also like an overall assumption and lack of role models,” she says.
	

	“The Difficult Bride” is an international co-production between France’s Les Films de l’Après-Midi, Bangladesh’s Khona Talkies, Portugal’s Midas Filmes, Norway’s Barentsfilm and Germany’s Tandem Production, and was supported by the first edition of the Fondazione Prada Film Fund. Films Boutique is handling world sales. Following Venice, the film moves on to the Toronto and BFI London film festivals. 

	For Hossain, the film marked a creative turning point. “I’m not tied to social realism anymore,” she says. “I really relied on my body and my instincts to make creative decisions, and I really enjoyed the process.” 

	She is now developing a project set in Lisbon about an undocumented Bangladeshi woman who migrates after a cyclone, and is pursuing a television adaptation of J. Courtney Sullivan’s novel “The Cliffs.”

title: ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Review: The ‘Free Solo’ Directors Return With Another Extreme Sports Doc, This Time Tainted by Tragedy
description: “Because it’s there” is the famous, possibly apocryphal, reply attributed to British mountaineer George Mallory when asked why he wanted to climb Mo
body:
“Because it’s there” is the famous, possibly apocryphal, reply attributed to British mountaineer George Mallory when asked why he wanted to climb Mount Everest. Unlike present-day climber Jim Morrison, Mallory didn’t also want to ski down it. But doesn’t the same non-answer apply? Why are certain people compelled toward any of these reckless, perilous, barely possible feats? If it’s just because they can, should they? These are the questions that will be on the minds of many viewers watching “Everest: The Other Side,” a gleaming, would-be rousing documentary portrait of Morrison, his late partner Hilaree Nelson, and a shared Everest ski-mountaineering dream that wound up taking her life. 
	

	But those questions are weakly and only intermittently asked by Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, the formerly married duo who won an Oscar for the giddy spectacle of “Free Solo,” their 2018 film about the similarly ambitious daredevil rock climber Alex Honnold. “Everest: The Other Side” aims for that film’s level of slack-jawed exhilaration: Everest itself is shot with sweeping, reverential grandeur, as it can hardly fail to be; Morrison’s eventual hard-won scaling of it is triumphantly depicted, as is his wild, gliding descent. But it’s hard to thrill to any of this when our minds are on the woman who died attempting to do the same thing, and the children she left behind. To Morrison, as well as to the filmmakers, this awful backstory makes something cathartic of his accomplishment. Many in the audience, however, will query the point of it all.


	Nelson, in fact, was more self-searching than the film around her — which began development as a markedly different story, following the couple’s joint thrill-seeking mission with the same degree of awed excitement that colored “Free Solo’s” portrayal of Honnold. “People ask, ‘How do you find the balance,’ and I want to punch them,” says Nelson in interview footage, referring to the conflict she felt between her maternal obligations to her sons Grayden and Quinn, 11 and 13 respectively at the start of filming, and her urge to follow her bliss as a ski-mountaineer, knowing the dangers involved. Later, she resumes the subject: “What I can do is love my kids today when I see them. What else can I do?”
	

	Those words haunt proceedings after, around the half-hour mark, Vasarhelyi and Chin reveal her fate: On September 26, 2022, while skiing with Morrison in Nepal, Nelson was caught in a small avalanche, and fell nearly 6,000 feet to her death. It’s a turn of events that the film rather distastefully presents as a twist, having hitherto given no indication to the uninformed that Nelson — seemingly a vibrant, driving subject of the story — is no longer with us. But even if you know what’s coming, it’s a wrench, of the kind that you think might steer “Everest: The Other Side” into more introspective territory. The filmmakers were close friends of the couple: Surely, one thinks, they must have complex feelings about their role in documenting the primal adrenalin rush of such sports over their self-serving riskiness, just as Morrison, in the wake of the tragedy, may wonder what it was all for.

	But if these concerns are felt, they’re barely admitted, as the remainder of the documentary celebrates determination over doubt, finding first a spiritual victory in continuing the quest, and a physical one in completing it. The show must go on, even if said show is skiing down the north face of Everest — something that has never been done before, which in the circumstances, wouldn’t strike most people as a good enough reason to do it. Morrison, whom we gradually learn has experienced more bereavement by tragic misadventure than any one man should bear, is fixated on the idea that securing this world-first would be both a personal vindication and a tribute to the memories of those he’s lost.

	In his state of mourning, one can see how this narrative might make sense. But the film co-signs it with a strangely gung-ho spirit, as Chin — himself a father of two — joins the mission with scant discussion of the potential hubris of this decision. Vasarhelyi, seemingly a less hands-on presence in this project, voices a few more misgivings, at one stage pointedly asking her husband how many people who have previously been guests at their dinner table are now dead. (It is not mentioned in the film, but the filmmakers filed for divorce last year.) But for the most part, “Everest: The Other Side” continues to track the progress of Morrison and Chin — accompanied by a sizable camera crew and a rather more circumspect team of sherpas whose voices are largely sidelined — as though chronicling a nobly epic expedition.
	

	And if you allow yourself to be guided only by the film’s stunning mountain vistas — those vast slopes, the uninterrupted pelt of brilliant snow atop them, the neon-yellow punctuation marks of the men’s tents and gear — and the full-tilt orchestral push of Caroline Ho’s score, you might get caught up in the romantic, near-fantastical folly of the enterprise, as befits a film presented, like much of Vasarhelyi and Chin’s previous work, under the National Geographic documentary banner. 

	But that requires significant compartmentalization of information that “Everest: The Other Side” has already offered us: the death of Nelson, the heartbroken testimonials of her now near-adult children, and a near-fatal injury sustained on the venture by Nepalese guide Pur Bahadur “Yukta” Gurung. (In a further gut-punch, the closing credits feature a posthumous tribute to Gurung: He died in an avalanche just a month before the doc’s Venice premiere.) It’s difficult to feel overly inspired by the eventual capture of a thrill that has fatally escaped many others; we’re simply left to wonder where Morrison’s insatiable yen will lead him next, and whether that, for better or worse, will be the final summit.

schema.headline: ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Review: The ‘Free Solo’ Directors Return With Another Extreme Sports Doc, This Time Tainted by Tragedy

title: Lav Diaz Preps False Prophets Film and Jose Rizal’s ‘Noli Me Tangere’ Adaptation, Unpacks Venice Title ‘Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Lav Diaz is developing a film about false prophets and a screen adaptation of José Rizal’s “Noli Me Tangere,” the Filipino auteur reveals, alongside
body:
Lav Diaz is developing a film about false prophets and a screen adaptation of José Rizal’s “Noli Me Tangere,” the Filipino auteur reveals, alongside details on “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” (“Makikiraan Po”), his Spanish colonization drama premiering in the Venice Open section of the Venice Film Festival.

	Diaz tells Variety, “Right now, I’m working on a film that discourses on false ideologies and false prophets.” He is also developing a separate project drawing on the writing of “Noli Me Tangere,” the Rizal novel credited with helping inspire the Philippine Revolution of 1896.
	

	Diaz shared those plans alongside a discussion of “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors,” which marks a return to Venice for the director. He won the festival’s Golden Lion in 2016 for “The Woman Who Left.” He arrives with the film following “Magellan,” which stars Gael Garcia Bernal as the Portuguese explorer and premiered at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival.


	“Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors,” for which Variety is unveiling a trailer, marks Diaz’s third excursion into a specific historical epoch, following “A Lullaby to the Sorrowful Mystery,” anchored in the Philippine Revolution of 1896. This time, Diaz reaches further back, to the late 16th century and early 17th century, when Spanish forces under Miguel Lopez de Legazpi consolidated colonial rule after Legazpi’s 1565 arrival in Cebu, 44 years after Magellan first landed in the archipelago. Chieftain Rajah Tupas resisted the Spanish for nearly a month before Legazpi bombarded local villages, forcing Tupas into a settlement.

	“It is an essential part of my continuing studies and dissection of my people’s struggle, or simply trying to understand the history of the Philippines,” Diaz says.
	

	The film centers on the forced labor used to build the Philippines’ colonial-era churches, structures Diaz argues are steeped in violence despite their standing today as celebrated cultural and religious landmarks. Under Spanish rule, able-bodied Malay men, from teenagers to adults, were required to perform 40 days of unpaid annual labor on roads, bridges, churches, forts, piers, plantations, haciendas and mines.

	“Forgetful Filipinos must learn, must know, must understand, that these structures were built by forced labor, and that they didn’t appear in their midst by some cosmic manifestations — it’s blood, sweat, tears, and deaths of our ancestors,” Diaz says.

	He adds that, based on historical accounts, around 30% of the male population perished under the forced-labor system.

	Diaz extends that critique of institutional power to religion itself. “Religion is one of the worst forms of violence,“ he says. “Faith can be a form of eternal subjugation, especially for the weak. Oftentimes, it blurs all of rationality; it becomes the truth of existence.” He points to the Crusades and the Holocaust as historical examples, and cites present-day conflicts in Gaza, Ukraine, Afghanistan and Darfur as evidence of faith’s continuing entanglement with violence.

	The film’s Filipino title — “Makikiraan Po” — comes from a phrase still used today by Filipino Malays passing through places believed to hold ancestral spirits. “I still do it, naturally, when I am entering a forest, a zone, when I am thinking of the unattainable,” Diaz says. “It is a connection, a relationship, with the ancient, with the primal, the pure.”

	Diaz also traces the roots of the Philippines’ present-day class structure to the encomienda system, which King Philip II ordered Legazpi to impose in 1571. Under the system, indigenous communities lost ownership of their land while paying heavy tributes and performing forced labor for Spanish encomenderos. He says, “All the old rich families, landlords, hacienderos, political clans, big businesses, have their connection from the encomienda.”

	Diaz shot “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” in black and white in Sampaloc, Quezon Province, marking his fourth production in the town, following “Magellan,” “Phantosmia” and the upcoming “Kawalan.” He credits the area with restoring his health after tuberculosis burst his left lung following the editing of “Magellan,” and again after he was later afflicted with severe asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
	

	“The spirit of the place provides the best attributes I needed in my films on issues of truth, vision and transcendence,” he says.

	Diaz cast filmmaker Isabel Sandoval, known for her own distinctive body of work, alongside longtime collaborators Ronnie Lazaro and Yul Servo. Sandoval plays the Babaylan, a traditional Malay healer who Diaz describes as a lasting bridge between Filipinos and their pre-Hispanic, pre-Islamic Malay heritage.

	Diaz says, “She contributed majestic nuance in the whole vision of the Babaylan character, and I am truly grateful for her generosity.”

	At 151 minutes, “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” runs shorter than many of the films Diaz is best known for, though he says his process didn’t change. “Nothing really changed with my praxis,” he says. “My principle has always been to work on the demands of the material at hand, to work around the conditions and situations. There’s never a fixed setup or framework. It’s just all hard work on the different aspects of the process really. The struggle to pursue a vision is the most important.”

	He adds: “Cinema must have the responsibility to commit to the truth. There should be no compromise on that issue given the condition of the world right now. Cinema’s soul is the truth.”

	“Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” is produced by C’est Lovi Prods., Epicmedia Prods. and Sine Olivia Pilipinas, with Heretic handling world sales.

title: Swiss Projects at the Venice Gap-Financing Market: Natural Disaster, Complicated Romance, Exploited Migrants, Murder Mystery in Montana
description: Both well-established and up-and-coming Swiss filmmakers are taking part in the Venice Film Festival’s Production Bridge industry strand, where Swit
body:
Both well-established and up-and-coming Swiss filmmakers are taking part in the Venice Film Festival’s Production Bridge industry strand, where Switzerland will be one of the country’s in focus at the Gap-Financing Market.

	Seven Swiss projects and co-productions are among the total of 38 fiction and documentary works featured in the Venice Production Bridge’s Gap-Financing Market lineup, selected from a record-breaking 370-plus submissions.
	

	Spanning a wide range of subject matter and genre, the projects, in various stages of development, delve into the human toll of natural cataclysm, the forced criminality of migration, cross-cultural  and cross-class romance, murder mystery, apocalyptic sci-fi and the artistic process.


	Among them are works by Flurin Giger, who premiered his 2016 short “Ruah” in Venice and 2018’s “Schächer” in Cannes; award-winning filmmaker Stéphanie Argerich with her first narrative feature; Valentin Merz, who picked up a first feature prize in Locarno in 2022 for “De noche los gatos son pardos”; Ursula Meier, whose credits include the 2012 and 2022 Berlin-premiering, prize-winning works “Sister” and “The Line“; and Kaveh Bakhtiari, who follows up his acclaimed 2013 Cannes doc “Stop-Over” with his scripted feature debut.

	Giger arrives with “A Year Without Summer,” produced by Geneva-based Beauvoir Films and Heimatfilm in Cologne. Set in 1816, it follows a peasant family in Europe whose existence is threatened when the skies suddenly darken and snow falls in the midst of summer. Unbeknownst to them, they are experiencing the effects of a catastrophic volcanic eruption in Indonesia.
	

	“What immediately drew us to this project first was Flurin,” Beauvoir Films producer Cécile Tollu-Polonowski tells Variety. “We had seen both his shorts, ‘Ruah’ in Venice and ‘Schächer’ in Cannes Critics’ Week, worked with him as an actor for another production, and there is a very particular handwriting to how he tells a story, a visual language that is his alone. He’s one of the most exciting up-and-coming directors we know, and honestly his debut feature fits perfectly into Beauvoir’s line-up as we nourish the same desire for cinema.”

	The project stands apart through the extraordinary subject itself, Tollu-Polonowski adds. “It is based on a real event. In 1816, the world went dark after the eruption of volcano Tambora; it transformed the climate and reshaped lives across continents.

	“It’s a story that’s completely fascinating and evokes so many images. It’s an event that has inspired artists long before us. It was during this year that brought so much death and misery that painters like Caspar David Friedrich and J.M.W. Turner created some of their most celebrated works, skies with these strange, powerful colors, a rare kind of splendor. What they were painting was actually real, it was the atmospheric aftermath of the eruption.”

	Currently being cast with a mix of professional and non-professional actors, the film will shoot in Rhaeto-Romanic, spoken in parts of southeastern Switzerland and northeastern Italy.

	Beyond the historical setting, the story also offers frightening parallels to the present day, Tollu-Polonowski notes: “A world thrown off balance by something invisible, people trying to make sense of a changed climate. It doesn’t feel like a period piece.”

	After winning acclaim for her 2012 documentary “Bloody Daughter,” about her parents, renowned pianists Martha Argerich and Stephen Kovacevich, Argerich returns with narrative feature “Kyushu Moon,” produced by Geneva-based Intermezzo Films and Les Films du Bélier in Paris.

	The film centers on Sarah (played by Alba Rohrwacher), a recently divorced journalist who travels to Japan for a report on a retreat for men with relationship difficulties. There she meets Moroto (Ryo Kase), a 42-year-old virgin man. Despite not speaking each other’s language, unexpected feelings arise.
	

	Argerich has re-teamed with Intermezzo Films’ Luc Peter and Katia Monla, who also produced “Bloody Daughter.”

	“We love her energy, the way she looks at her surroundings with an attention to detail, and how, in the smallest unnoticed gesture, an emotion can surface, revealing our fragilities through a gaze that never judges, but simply recognizes our human failures,” says Monla.

	“What drew us to ‘Kyushu Moon’ was the way it questions our modern solitude: our loss of connection in a fast-paced society, our relationship to others, to another culture, at a time when everything seems to be pushing us toward individuality and a closing off from the world, from the other, from what is strange and foreign.

	“It is, in that sense, a political film about a declining demographic left to fend for itself, and about how, in an unexpected setting, two people meet and find themselves able to imagine a relationship to the other again, just when everything seemed lost. But beneath its political and social surface, it remains, at heart, a deeply poetic romance laced with a touch of humor, a bridge between Europe and Asia, where two lost souls find a way to hope again.”

	“Kyushu Moon” is set to begin its six-week shoot in Beppu, Japan, in October.

	The Swiss projects in the Venice Gap-Financing Market also include:

	“Chocolat Amer,” by Valentin MerzCinédokké Sagl, Andrea Film (Switzerland), Unafilm (Germany)Sadek, a young Tunisian in Zurich, becomes the lover of a chocolate heir while the world’s cacao is dying. The closer he comes to the Perret family and their synthetic chocolate, the more he transforms — until his body and his sense of self begin to slip away from him.

	“Quiet Land,” by Ursula MeierBande à part Films (Switzerland), Paradise City (France)

	Ageing Montana Highway Patrol Officer Connor McCluskey is investigating two puzzling fatal car crashes. After being dismissed from the force, he worries the same fate may befall a woman who owns land in the same area. Has he uncovered an inexplicable criminal plot, or is he slowly losing his mind?

	“Salut Robert,” by Laura IsraelCorrespondent Productions (U.S.), Mira Films (Switzerland), 4 A 4 Productions (France)

	A diaristic portrait of photographer and filmmaker Robert Frank, best known for his pictures of a postwar America riven by social and political discord, the film spans nearly half a century, assembled from unseen personal footage and home movies, offering a time capsule of a vibrant and tumultuous time in social and art history.

	“The Rope,” by Alberto FasuloNefertiti Film (Italy), Beauvoir Films (Switzerland)
	

	When Pawl chooses to awaken from the artificial sleep that the rest of humanity finds itself in, he is exiled back to a devastated planet, an uninhabited land shrouded in fog. There, he will rediscover the importance of bonds and hope for humankind.

	“The Smuggler,” by Kaveh BakhtiariBeauvoir Films (Switzerland),  Homemade Films (Greece), TS Productions (France) 

	Ali, a 16-year-old Afghan migrant, has found refuge in a salon in Athens, where he cuts hair and does odd jobs to survive, only to suddenly find himself propelled into the world of smugglers and counterfeiters. The humanity behind the darkness of forced criminal exploitation “drew me to create a sober narrative capable of capturing the density of the circumstances,” says Bakhtiari, an Iranian native and exile himself who previously explored the undocumented migrant experience in “Stop-Over.”

schema.headline: Swiss Projects at the Venice Gap-Financing Market: Natural Disaster, Complicated Romance, Exploited Migrants, Murder Mystery in Montana

title: Mad Solutions and Haitham Dabbour’s Irth Platform Announce Strategic Pan-Arab Content Partnership in Venice
description: Pan-Arab distributor Mad Solutions and Egyptian multihyphenate Haitham Dabbour’s Irth platform dedicated to supporting standout writers across the A
body:
Pan-Arab distributor Mad Solutions and Egyptian multihyphenate Haitham Dabbour’s Irth platform dedicated to supporting standout writers across the Arab world announced a strategic partnership on Saturday at the Venice Film Festival that aims to boost quality content output from the region.

	Under the pact, Mad Solutions and Irth will jointly “develop, package and support film, television and other entertainment projects from across the Arab world for regional and international markets,” they said in a statement.
	

	The Irth platform initiative – that was officially launched during the 2025 Red Sea International Film Festival in Saudi Arabia – is the first collaborative writers’ room bringing together writers from Egypt and Saudi Arabia and beyond.


	Cairo-based Mad Solutions, which was established in 2010 by its two co-founders, Alaa Karkouti and Maher Diab, comprises a network of specialized outfits that include Mad World, focussed on international sales of Arab films; Mad Distribution, which handles sales and distribution of Arab films across the Arab world; and Mad Celebrity, providing full talent management and representation for both on-and off-screen Arab talent.

	MAD Solutions and Irth are now developing a pipeline spanning original Arabic projects, some of which are talent-driven, as well as third-party development and consultancy assignments. The first projects germinated from the partnership will be announced, they said.

	The partnership announcement comes just as Mad Solutions marks a significant presence in Venice this year, with two films launching on the Lido. “Al Baraneya,” a rural Egyptian family’s story directed by Egypt’s Ashgan El-Hamus, screening in Venice Days, and Palestinian drama “Conversations with the Sea,” directed by Muayad Alayan, screening in the Venice Spotlight section. 
	

	MAD will also present its annual award at the Final Cut in Venice platform, which supports films from Africa and the Arab world through post-production and international industry opportunities.

	Dabbour is a bestselling Egyptian author whoser novels include “Devoured by Seven Lean Cows” and “Moses Cross.” His screenwriting credits include Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival prizewinner “Gunshot” and “The Tale of Ahl El Daye,” which in 2025 had its European bow in the Berlinale’s Generation section.

	“Irth has always been about bringing strong writers and different Arab voices together and giving ideas the development they need,” Dabbour in a statement. “Mad’s regional and international reach gives us the opportunity to take that work further and open new possibilities for the projects and writers we work with.”

	Commented Mad Solutions co-founders Alaa Karkouti and Maher Diab: “Development is a key part of Mad’s regional and international expansion, and Irth brings a strong creative infrastructure and a diverse network of Arab writers to that strategy. Together, we can originate projects while also offering filmmakers and producers the development support they need to strengthen existing ones.”

schema.headline: Mad Solutions and Haitham Dabbour’s Irth Platform Announce Strategic Pan-Arab Content Partnership in Venice

title: Convicted Tupac Shakur Killer Duane Davis Says He Wasn't Even at the Crime Scene
description:
Tupac Shakur Killer Duane Davis
                          How Many Damn Times Do I Have to Say It
body:
Tupac Shakur Killer Duane Davis
                          How Many Damn Times Do I Have to Say It?
                          'I'm Innocent, Man'!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 5, 2026
                            2:48 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Convicted Tupac Shakur killer Duane "Keffe D" Davis is maintaining his innocence ahead of his sentencing, saying he didn't do "s—t" and wasn't anywhere near the murder scene.
      
    
            Davis was interviewed by the Hollywood Reporter for an article published Friday after he was recently convicted of the 1996 murder of the iconic rapper during a drive by shooting in Las Vegas. At his trial, prosecutors said Davis did not pull the trigger but passed a gun to the shooter, who then pumped Tupac full of bullets.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Davis told the Hollywood Reporter ... "I’m innocent, man. They got an innocent man sitting in jail." But he vowed to be released from prison, saying he had already filed an appeal with the state court.
      

            Davis said he's confident he'll win his appeal because the state authorities violated a non-prosecution agreement he had with the feds to tell them what happened the night Tupac was killed.  Davis also said, "The DOJ gave me a deal ... It came from the top and they said that they was never going to use it in court against me."
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            During a 2008 interview with the feds, Davis confessed that he orchestrated the Tupac murder by getting hold of the gun and then "hunting" down Tupac and Marion "Suge Knight after the two beat up Davis' cousin earlier in the night. Davis' trial attorney told the jury that his client was just bragging and trying to make money off his book by telling lies.
      
    
            In addition, Davis told the Hollywood Reporter that he wasn't even at the crime scene that night, adding that he went to a bar near UCLA in Los Angeles after attending the Mike Tyson boxing match at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas. The next morning, Davis said, he returned home to have breakfast with his son and daughters.
      
    
            Davis is scheduled to be sentenced on October 13.

schema.headline: Convicted Tupac Shakur Killer Duane Davis Says He Wasn't Even at the Crime Scene

title: Burning Man Attendee Dies After Medical Emergency at Nevada Festival
description:
Burning Man
                          Participant Dies at Festival
body:
Burning Man
                          Participant Dies at Festival
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A man is dead after suffering a medical emergency at the Burning Man festival in Nevada.
      
    
            Organizers say the man, who was in his mid-50s, became sick Thursday at the Black Rock Desert event. He was treated with lifesaving measures before being transported to the festival's emergency care center, where he was pronounced dead.
      
    
            The death comes as heavy rain forced officials to close the festival's main entrance and exit gate. Organizers urged people planning to attend to delay their travel ... while those already at the event were told to avoid driving.
      
    
            The incident also comes one year after the death of 37-year-old Vadim Kruglov, who was found fatally stabbed inside a tent at Burning Man in August 2025.
      
    
            Kruglov’s death was considered the first recorded homicide in the festival's history.

title: L.A. Rams’ Aaron Donald Alleges Ex Warned Their Kids Not To ‘Run Their Mouths’ About Dog
description:
L.A. Rams’ Aaron Donald
                          Claims Ex Told Their Kids Not to ‘Run Their Mou
body:
L.A. Rams’ Aaron Donald
                          Claims Ex Told Their Kids Not to ‘Run Their Mouths’
                          About ‘Dangerous’ Bulldog
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Aaron Donald feared his ex Jaelynn Blakey’s dog may harm their kids and rushed to court weeks before the NFL season starts, TMZ has learned. 
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Aaron, who shares two minor kids with Jaelynn, requested primary custody until the dog was removed from Jaelynn’s home. The California Post was the first to report the news. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Aaron said their kids were in immediate danger each time they were at her home and came close to the French bulldog. 
      

            In his filing, Aaron said the dog has bitten both children, as well as his ex’s niece, who was 10 at the time. 
      
    
            Aaron said his ex told him she was removing the dog, but he later learned the dog came back to the home after being at another home for a couple of months.
      
    
            The NFL star said Jaelynn denied the kids were scared of the dog or that the animal was dangerous.
      
    
            In a declaration, Aaron claimed his kids told him Jaelynn told them not to “run their mouths” by telling him about the dog being back. 
      
    
            Jaelynn denied she ever told the kids to lie to their dad. She said the NFL star is “taking away the family pet” who had been around for years. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In her court docs, she said, “He does this under the guise of protecting the children and their safety but that is not his true intent as evidenced by the fact that the dog has lived in my home over the past several years."
      
    
            Jaelynn said the dog was her “emotional support” animal and was loved by the kids. 
      
    
            On August 3, the exes reached a deal where Jaelynn agreed to get rid of the dog once and for all.

title: Aaron Rodgers Hopes to Start Family After Retirement From NFL
body:
Aaron Rodgers
                          Ready for Fatherhood!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 4, 2026
                            5:45 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Aaron Rodgers is looking forward to retirement ... and says he hopes to start a family with his wife.
      
    
            The Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback opened up about his future during an interview with SiriusXM's "Mad Dog Sports Radio," saying he's hoping to be "supporting my pregnant wife" by this time next year.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Rodgers said he and his wife, publicly known as Brittani, plan to start a family after he steps away from football following the 2026 season.
      
    
            "I'm looking forward to a life of quiet after 22 years in the pros and three in college," he said ... adding he's also focused on healing his body and building a family.
      

            Rodgers later clarified he and Brittani are not currently expecting but said fatherhood is the next chapter he’s most excited about.
      
    
            He says he enjoys being "Uncle Aaron" to his brother's children and said spending time with them has made both him and his wife more eager to have kids of their own.
      
    
            Rodgers confirmed in May the 2026 NFL season will be his last. He previously revealed he secretly married Brittani in 2025 ... but has kept details about their relationship largely private.
